title: Triangle Centers, Ceva, Menelaus & Stewart Theorem

sections.heading: Triangle Centers, Ceva, Menelaus & Stewart Theorem Practice Exercises

questions.q: In \( \triangle ABC \) shown, points \( D \in BC \), \( E \in CA \), and \( F \in AB \) are chosen so that the cevians \( AD, BE, CF \) concur at an interior point \( P \). Given \( \frac{BD}{DC} = \frac{1}{2} \) and \( \frac{CE}{EA} = \frac{1}{3} \), find \( \frac{AF}{FB} \).
questions.answer: By Ceva's Theorem on concurrent cevians \( AD, BE, CF \), \[ \frac{AF}{FB} \cdot \frac{BD}{DC} \cdot \frac{CE}{EA} = 1 \implies \frac{AF}{FB} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1 \implies \frac{AF}{FB} = 6. \]

questions.q: Point \( D \) lies on the extension of side \( BC \) of \( \triangle ABC \) beyond \( C \) such that \( BC = 3 \) and \( CD = 2 \). A line through \( D \) intersects segment \( AB \) at \( F \) with \( \frac{AF}{FB} = \frac{2}{2} \) and intersects segment \( AC \) at \( E \). By Menelaus's Theorem, find \( \frac{CE}{EA} \).
questions.answer: First note the full exterior distance \( BD = BC + CD = 3 + 2 = 5 \) (using \( BC \) instead of \( BD \) is the classic Menelaus error). Applying Menelaus's Theorem to \( \triangle ABC \) and transversal \( F-E-D \) gives \[ \frac{AF}{FB} \cdot \frac{BD}{DC} \cdot \frac{CE}{EA} = 1 \implies \frac{2}{2} \cdot \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{CE}{EA} = 1 \implies \frac{CE}{EA} = \frac{2}{5}. \]

questions.q: In \( \triangle ABC \), the circumcircle \( (O) \) has radius \( R = 5 \) and the incircle \( (I) \) has radius \( r = 2 \). By Euler's Theorem in geometry, what is the exact squared distance \( OI^2 \) between the circumcenter and incenter?
questions.answer: By Euler's Triangle Theorem (proved by Power of Point \( I \) with respect to \( (O) \) and Fact 5 on the arc midpoint), \[ OI^2 = R(R - 2r) = 5(5 - 2 \cdot 2) = 5 \cdot 1 = 5. \]

questions.q: In \( \triangle ABC \) shown, \( BC = 5 \), \( CA = 7 \), and \( AB = 6 \). Point \( D \) lies on side \( BC \) with \( BD = 2 \) and \( DC = 3 \). Using Stewart's Theorem, compute \( AD^2 \).
questions.answer: Let \( d = AD \). Applying the Law of Cosines to supplementary angles at \( D \) yields Stewart's Theorem \[ AC^2 \cdot BD + AB^2 \cdot DC = BC(AD^2 + BD \cdot DC). \] Substituting \( 7^2(2) + 6^2(3) = 5(d^2 + 2\cdot 3) \) gives \( 5d^2 = 176 \), hence \( AD^2 = \frac{176}{5} \).
